prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, a general and ligand-controlled method for constructing arylamines

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B035 with Buchwald and Hartwig. After the first round the case rests on three points that no one has contested on scientific grounds. First, the chemistry is new: reductive elimination from a palladium amido complex was the hard step, and it was solved by ligand design (bulky biaryl phosphines and chelating bisphosphines), so C-N coupling is a separate achievement from the C-C couplings honoured in 2010. Second, it is mature in the strongest sense, with three decades of independent use in medicinal chemistry, process chemistry and materials, visible in a vast number of later syntheses. Third, attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: every member who ranked B035 proposed the same two names. The chair's summary shows that no configuration has more than two explicit supporters, so I have asked which of the alternatives I could genuinely support if B035 does not carry. I could accept B010 once the committee confirms the clinical and expert-report picture and settles the third name; I could accept B011 on a two-person Balasubramanian and Klenerman citation. I do not move either ahead of B035 now, because B035 carries neither a maturity risk nor an attribution dispute.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are the 2010 prize and Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling. I answer the first on the chemistry, but I accept that a committee wanting breadth across sub-fields may see another palladium prize as repetitive. On Kosugi, a precursor that used stoichiometric tin amides and was not a general catalytic method is better handled by a careful citation and by Buchwald and Hartwig's independent catalytic, ligand-enabled work than by a third laureate; if the expert report finds Kosugi's claim stronger than I judge, the three-name limit is strained. B035 is also less conceptually sweeping than degraders or sequencing, and it has less reach outside chemistry, so it may simply rank behind them for members who weight breadth over depth.

responses.point: Chabes argues that B010 turns the ubiquitin-proteasome system into a designable chemical reaction, with reproducibility across many groups and an approved glue-class precedent, and he concedes that credit is split between PROTAC and glue strands.
responses.response: I accept the reproducibility and that the principle is general. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: a citation covering both strands is stitching, and a PROTAC-only citation leaves the best-validated medicines unexplained. If the committee can write one honest sentence with a justified third name, I would support B010 as my first alternative. As things stand I also want the expert report on the state of late-stage degrader trials before I rank it above a method whose impact is already complete. The question for me is whether the prize would recognise what has been delivered or what is expected.

responses.point: Aili ranks B010 first with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and treats induced proximity as a chemical design principle that reaches formerly undruggable targets.
responses.response: The design-principle argument is fair, and I withdraw part of my first-round objection that this is only chemical biology: linker, ligand and ternary-complex design are real molecule-making. I still note that the concept is event-driven pharmacology applied through an existing biological machine, whereas C-N coupling created a bond-forming reaction that did not exist in usable form. Your own case_against concedes the heterobifunctional approval gap. I would not oppose B010 in the final vote if B035 falls short, but I ask you to say whether Handa or Ciulli is the better third name, since that choice decides which strand the prize honours.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers B011 narrowed to Balasubramanian and Klenerman, a single sequencing-by-synthesis lineage, as the clearest game-changer with no maturity risk.
responses.response: Your narrowing to two names answers the attribution objection I raised in round 1, and I now regard B011 as a credible configuration. My remaining concern is category: reversible terminators and clustering are real chemistry, but sequencing as a platform sits close to medicine and physiology, and Rothberg's and Mayer's exclusion will be argued. I also think you understate how much a clean two-name prize matters: B035 has the same maturity as B011 and a cleaner attribution record. I would rank B011 as my second alternative and could support it if the expert report treats the terminator chemistry as the decisive step.

responses.point: Linke ranked B035 eighth, citing reluctance to honour another cross-coupling after 2010, and his own first choice is B046, where he accepts that the in-cell claims are unsettled.
responses.response: The chair's summary frames the 2010 overlap as an open dispute, so I will restate it briefly: Heck, Negishi and Suzuki couplings join carbon to carbon through transmetalation, whereas C-N coupling depends on amine binding, deprotonation and reductive elimination from an amido complex, which is why it needed different ligands and arrived later. On B046, I accept the in vitro thermodynamic framework, but I agree with your own admission that the physiological claims are unsettled. The prize would be crediting a principle whose cellular role is still contested. Until the committee separates the two, I cannot rank it above a method with decades of independent confirmation.

responses.point: Brzezinski shares B035 with the same pair and treats Kosugi as a priority question that could strain the three-name limit, while asking for an organometallic expert report.
responses.response: I agree with your caution about Kosugi and about expert confirmation. My reading is that Kosugi's stoichiometric tin-amide precedent should appear in the citation or the background note as precedent and does not justify a third laureate, because the general catalytic method with ligand control, the thing that made C-N coupling a routine tool, was built by Buchwald and Hartwig. I would not seek to rest the case on your agreement alone: I would rely on the expert report to confirm that later ligand developers are not owed equal credit, and I would accept its finding if it differs from mine.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats C-N coupling as a distinct achievement from the 2010 prize, or as an extension of it, which for some members would decide the vote.
Whether Kosugi's tin-amide precedent is only a precursor or a priority claim strong enough to require a third name or a different citation.
Whether B010 will be mature enough in clinical terms, and whether Handa or Ciulli fits a combined PROTAC and glue citation, which determines whether I would move it up in the final vote.

Whether a synthetic-methodology prize can reach a majority of five when no configuration has more than two explicit supporters; I have not settled how to weigh breadth of reach against depth and attribution if B035 falls short.
My view of Pd-catalysed amination reflects the literature as I recall it, not the expert reports, which I have not read.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I trained with Masamune at MIT and have no known personal or institutional tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi, nor to any other shortlisted candidate. I share a university and department context with Heiner Linke and Emma Sparr at Lund, but none of the shortlisted candidates is from Lund, and I do not consider this a ground for recusal.
